descendants.title: A child failure can spend a fresh-launch budget
descendants.child: startup.childFailureRetryLimit · 1 retry · Explicit startup child failure · Preserve one fresh launch after a failed child
descendants.prediction: A child exits during startup. Must “no healthy-startup deadline” mean wait forever, or can startup launch again?
descendants.assessment: New consequence on descent. P2 announces absent warm-up and silence deadlines; P9 names two accepted-execution counters. Neither carries this third, startup-specific budget. “Startup” in the family list does not identify the trigger or the relaunch.
descendants.repair: A startup child failure can consume a separate fresh-launch allowance; the default permits one retry. Ownership waits do not reset the counter. This is separate from healthy warm-up having no deadline.
descendants.reason: Stated: the policy record preserves one fresh launch after a failed child. PR #131 routes attempts through policy.

descendants.title: One shutdown family contains different wait boundaries
descendants.child: shutdown.stopTimeoutMs · Bound graceful stop and forced escalation together; recipe.forcedTerminationReserve · min(maximum, floor(stopTimeoutMs / 2)); processSignalExitTimeoutMs · 500 ms after SIGTERM and 500 ms after SIGKILL
descendants.prediction: A test reduces the stop budget below one second. Does force still reserve a full 500 ms? Does this also change the two signal-exit waits?
descendants.assessment: New relationships on descent. Other fronts name acceptance-based idle timing, bounded ACK waits, and force escalation. They do not identify the stop-budget/reserve coupling or distinguish it from per-signal termination waits. The missing information is more than the spelling or exact value of a field.
descendants.repair: User stop shares one budget between graceful work and forced escalation; force reserves at most half that budget, capped by policy. Direct SIGTERM and SIGKILL each have their own exit wait. Idle lifetime and drain acknowledgement have separate clocks.
descendants.reason: Stated: the policy record explains bounded stop, preserving small overridden stop windows, and a bounded wait for each signal.

descendants.title: Memory limits do not identify the two sampling jobs
descendants.child: resources.supervisionIntervalMs · Process RSS and spool sampling · Detect sustained pressure; resources.workerHeapSampleIntervalMs · Active worker heap high-water sampling · Observe short-lived heap peaks
descendants.prediction: If an active worker has a short heap peak between process samples, which other measurement is intended to observe it?
descendants.assessment: New relationship on descent. P3 gives derivation, clamps and hysteresis; Q2/Q5 give a turn-boundary sample and the last sampled values. None announces the separate active-worker high-water cadence. The table names two observers with different purposes.
descendants.repair: Process supervision samples RSS and spool state; a separate, faster active-worker sampler observes heap high-water. Replacement count and time window bound churn independently of both cadences.
descendants.reason: Stated: the policy record separately explains sustained-pressure sampling, short heap peaks, and replacement churn.

descendants.title: Diagnostic history and pending writes consume different capacity
descendants.child: diagnostics.logRotateBytes / logBackupCount · Bounded diagnostic history; diagnostics.maximumQueuedEvents · Pending diagnostic writes · Bound memory when storage is slow
descendants.prediction: Does bounding retained log files also explain what limits memory while diagnostic writes are queued behind slow storage?
descendants.assessment: The generic “diagnostics … retention/capacity limits” parent leaves the relationship underspecified. D4 separates traces from retained results, which is useful, but neither names the pending-write queue versus retained log files. This is a stricter semantic-parent reading than treating every diagnostic field as numeric fidelity.
descendants.repair: Diagnostics separately bound active/backup files, pending-write memory, and disconnected traces. Trace expiry does not evict results.
descendants.reason: Stated: the policy record distinguishes bounded history, slow-storage memory, and reconnect evidence.

descendants.title: The helper can make the directory before capture exists
descendants.child: The transport helper’s legacy-options path calls mkdirSync(outputDirectory, { recursive: true }) during construction.
descendants.prediction: The directory exists after helper construction and is empty at the end. Which component could have created it, even if the output never spilled?
descendants.assessment: A source descent adds a distinct cause. P7 already preserves the positive floor and empty-directory-without-spill warning. Its linked transport-helper source also creates the directory. The same side effect is present in the pinned #131 helper at lines 54–55, so this is not solely a later-stage difference.
descendants.repair: On the legacy-options path, transport construction creates the supplied output directory and floors inline storage at a chunk. Directory existence and later emptiness can both occur without file-backed capture.
descendants.reason: Unexplained: test-only tuning is stated, but no separate reason for constructor directory creation was located.

descendants.title: A positive floor is conditional, and helper precedence differs
descendants.child: Workspace helper: zero inline is mapped to a positive value only when a result bound is available; explicit policy is a base for legacy overlays. Transport has a direct-policy branch.
descendants.prediction: Can every zero-inline legacy option become valid? Do explicit policy and legacy options always merge in the same way?
descendants.assessment: P7’s “may” correctly avoids promising universal zero repair. It still does not let a reader predict the controlling result-bound condition or override precedence. The linked process-helper keeps that condition; #131’s workspace helper shows it at lines 37–51. The exact cross-helper precedence comparison is supplied by #131 sources and 52 D29.
descendants.repair: Workspace zero-inline repair requires a result bound and also reduces the chunk cap. It overlays legacy options on a base policy. Other wrappers can prefer explicit policy or take a direct-policy path. “Adapter” does not imply one universal merge rule.
descendants.reason: Unexplained: positive ordered capacities and test-only adaptation are stated; the exact translations and precedence choices lack separate reasons in the inspected record.

cases: A larger numeric limit does not itself install a repeated-fetch loop. The failed fetch calls fail and settles this attempt. A qualifying accepted-close failure may reach the separate outer reattachment path.
The same D06 parent and before/after mechanism are reachable in both layouts. This is a textual/source prediction, not a newly executed recovery trace.

Status-observer composition selects 100 ms; ordinary lifecycle/execution-status selects 250 ms. Admission has a separate 5 s timer ending at acceptance, so neither lifecycle wait bounds accepted navigation.
The diagram shows the owners; D04 supplies the selection rule. Gray import arrows alone cannot answer a runtime-deadline question.

The transport helper floors inline at 64 KiB and can create the directory before capture; one 64 KiB record can remain in memory. Empty afterward does not establish deletion of a spooled file. With workspace inline zero and result cap two, inline and chunk become one; two one-byte records cross the inline threshold.
D17/D19 were operated in both layouts; the shared source also supplies D18. This is an illustrative source-derived storage account, not a disk experiment.
First close, then a different completion error

At #131 head, failure while opening the next attachment preserves the preceding accepted-close error. After that attachment is accepted, a different completion failure can become the current error. Base rethrew the first accepted-close error in both cases.
D07 states this before descent in both layouts. 51’s R3 expressly describes superseding final-stack behavior; it cannot replace the #131 account.
